items.t: Guojin Securities' Mou Yiling: Blue-Chip Valuations Near Historic Lows, Three Themes to Capture Structural Opportunities in China's A-Shares
sum: From November 6 to 7, Mou Yiling, chief strategist and executive deputy director of the research institute at Guojin Securities, said in a media interview that China's A-share market has been under sustained pressure since mid-to-late September, with rising external uncertainty the core disturbance behind this round of adjustment. However, he believes that valuations of core blue-chip A-share stocks have already fallen into a historically low range, and that combined with the fundamental resilience shown in third-quarter earnings and a wave of buybacks by listed companies, the market's underlying logic remains solid.

On the sources of external risk, Mou offered two threads. The first is geopolitical and inflation pressure: US-Iran talks are progressing slowly, excessively high oil prices are raising inflation risk, and although US Treasury yields have pulled back they remain elevated, with expectations of tightening liquidity weighing broadly on valuations of global risk assets. The second is disruption to the AI industry narrative: as overseas AI tech giants, represented by large cloud providers, reported earnings one after another, and leading closed-source large-model developer Anthropic published its prospectus, market concerns about returns on AI industry investment have reignited. In addition, after the US midterm elections the Democratic Party won control of both chambers of Congress, creating a divided government between Congress and the White House, which has raised uncertainty over industrial policy expectations and further suppressed risk appetite.

In contrast to the external disturbances, the report card delivered by China's third-quarter A-share earnings shows demand-side support remains. Citing data, Mou noted that in the third quarter of 2026, cumulative year-on-year revenue growth for all A-share companies (excluding financials and real estate) reached 7.4%, up 0.2 percentage points from the second quarter.

China's Four Major A-Share Indexes Open Lower; AI Hardware Sector Leads Declines as Over 5,400 Stocks Fall
sum: On the morning of November 6, China's four major A-share indexes opened collectively lower. The Shanghai Composite Index fell 2.11%, the Shenzhen Component Index dropped 3.72%, the ChiNext Index declined 4.99%, and the STAR Composite Index slid 5.33%, with more than 5,400 stocks across the market losing ground.

On the board, AI hardware-related sectors led the declines. The CPO sector fell sharply, with TFC Communication, Zhongji Innolight and Eoptolink Technology all opening more than 10% lower, while Yuanjie Technology, Robotechnik and Focuslight Technologies posted some of the steepest drops, with Zhongji Innolight down more than 12%. The components sector also weakened, with Dongshan Precision and Aohong Electronics hitting the daily limit down, Xunjiexing and Mankun Technology falling more than 10%, and Sihui Fuji, Nanya New Material and Huazheng New Material following lower.

In contrast, the insurance and banking sectors bucked the trend, while the power sector rallied intraday, with Xinneng Shares hitting the daily limit up and Nanwang Technology, Lixin Energy and Huaneng Hydropower rising in sympathy.
As of press time, overall market sentiment remained weak, with capital clearly withdrawing from AI hardware and defensive sectors receiving some support.

sum: On the morning of November 4, China's three major A-share indices diverged, with the ChiNext Index briefly rising more than 1% intraday before pulling back. As of the midday close, the Shanghai Composite fell 0.1%, the Shenzhen Component rose 0.14%, the ChiNext Index rose 0.1%, and the STAR Composite rose 1.22%. Combined turnover in Shanghai and Shenzhen reached CNY 92.51 billion (approximately $13.84 billion) for the half-day, down CNY 6.75 billion (approximately $1.01 billion) from the prior session, with more than 3,700 stocks declining market-wide.

Market hotspots were concentrated in technology growth names. Robotics and physical AI concepts rebounded: Yongzhen Co. (603381.SS) posted a second straight limit-up, Fulai New Materials (605488.SS) and Zhongma Transmission (603767.SS) hit limit-up, and Suocheng Technology (688507.SS) surged the full 20% limit. Semiconductor equipment concepts were active, with Torrens up more than 15% and Jingyi Equipment (688652.SS) up more than 8%; chip names including Hengxuan Technology (688608.SS), Juxin Technology and Fengtiao Technology (688279.SS) also gained more than 10%. The AI comic drama theme churned higher, with Dasheng Culture (600892.SS), Zhewen Pictures (601599.SS) and Longban Media (605577.SS) all notching a third straight limit-up, while Yinli Media (603598.SS) and Decai Co. (605287.SS) recorded two limit-ups in three days. Recently listed new stocks were also active, with Beite Li up the full 20% limit and Makuang Co. posting a second straight limit-up.

On the downside, real estate, optical modules and chemical fiber/chemicals led declines, while consumer stocks swung lower, with Sunshine Dairy (001318.SZ), Juneyao Health (605388.SH), Quanyangquan (600189.SH) and Baiyang Co. (002696.SZ) all touching the limit-down. Stocks with the character "yang" (sheep) in their names weakened collectively, with Aoyang Health (002172.SZ), Sunshine Lighting (600261.SH), Sunshine Dairy and Baiyang Co. hitting limit-down.
On the outlook, brokerage institutions offered differing perspectives.

Shanghai Composite Climbs Nearly 1% as Beijing Weighs Fresh Stock Support After Record 12-Week Losing Streak
sum: SHANGHAI — Chinese stocks rose on Monday as investors bet on new government measures to support the market, offsetting disappointing official data showing the economy weakened in October.
The Shanghai Composite index was up 34.21 points, or 0.95%, at 3,633.23 in afternoon trading. The index had risen as much as 1.16% by the midday break.
Gains were stronger elsewhere. The Shenzhen Component index was up 2.39% at midday, while the ChiNext index of growth stocks jumped 3.28%.

The rally was driven by reports that China's central bank would meet with financial and securities regulators and major banks on Monday to study improving a relending program that helps fund share buybacks.
The meeting comes after Chinese stocks suffered a record 12-week losing streak, with the CSI 300 index recording its worst month in more than a decade in October.
Any new steps would add to stabilization efforts launched last month, which have so far failed to reverse the downturn amid weak domestic demand and concerns about AI-related earnings.
The People's Bank of China also moved to anchor short-term rates, shifting to a daily overnight repo operation at 1.25%, in a move compared to the U.S. Federal Reserve's approach.

China regulators act to support stocks after October slump, mainland media reports
sum: Chinese financial regulators are preparing to take action to stabilize the market after a sharp decline in A-shares during October, according to mainland media reports.

The reports said that the People’s Bank of China, the China Securities Regulatory Commission, and the National Financial Regulatory Administration will meet with major banks on Monday. The regulators are expected to discuss expanding capital market support tools, including optimizing special re-lending facilities for stock buybacks and share purchases.
The special re-lending facility is designed to help listed companies and major shareholders access low-cost funds to repurchase shares and bolster stock prices.
A-shares experienced a significant downturn in October, with major indices hitting new lows for the year.
The Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.44 percent to close at 3,599.00 points on the final trading day of October, dropping below the 3,600-point mark for the first time this year.

Growth and tech stocks led the slide, with the Shenzhen Component Index down 2.73 percent to 10,833.78, the ChiNext Index dropping 4.13 percent to 2,413.63, and the SSE Science and Technology Innovation Board 50 Index declining 4.66 percent to 1,421.31.

Declines were widespread across sectors, led by heavy sell-offs in tech and media shares. More than 4,600 stocks across the entire market recorded losses. Combined turnover on the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges reached 1.67 trillion yuan (HK$1.97 trillion) that day, up 117.9 billion yuan from the previous session.
